ai_definition.definition: For the purposes of this Handbook, the MindForge consortium focuses on two key characteristics to help practitioners consistently identify and manage AI: (1) AI learns and/or infers from inputs to generate output such as estimates, predictions, content, summaries, recommendations, or decisions; (2) AI excludes calculators or tools whose outputs are solely based on predefined programming or rules. These characteristics generalise MAS' proposed Guidelines definition: "AI includes use cases involving models or systems that learn and/or infer from inputs to generate outputs such as estimates, predictions, content, summaries, recommendations, or decisions that may influence physical or virtual environments, and vary in their levels of autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment. Calculators or tools whose outputs are solely based on predefined programming logic or rules would not be regarded as AI for the purpose of these Guidelines."

terms.definition: An AI model, which is a mathematical or logical representation mapping inputs to outputs, is the foundation of modern AI technology. An AI model is any model which meets the definition of AI. Models output estimates, forecasts, or projections related to real-world phenomena. E.g. A function predicting the likelihood of a borrower to default based on their credit history is a model. E.g. A Large Language Model (LLM) that predicts word tokens is a model.

source.quote: An AI model, which is a mathematical or logical representation mapping inputs to outputs, is the foundation of modern AI technology.

terms.definition: An AI system includes an AI model as well as other software components that allow models to be used in real-world applications. A system can contain many software features, and potentially many models that interact via software. E.g. a spreadsheet with user data plus a statistical model saved as a JSON file accessed through an IDE; an AI chatbot using an AI search engine to retrieve files based on user prompts; an agentic workflow of multiple orchestrated AI 'agents'.

source.quote: An AI system includes an AI model as well as other software components that allow models to be used in real-world applications.

terms.definition: An AI use case is the specific, real-world context in which an AI system is intentionally used. Use cases are crucial for understanding the impact, risks, and functioning of systems. E.g. Using AI to consider several data points about a customer to underwrite loan risk is a use case.

source.quote: An AI use case is the specific, real-world context in which an AI system is intentionally used.

scope_notes: The Handbook is addressed to all Financial Institutions (FIs) of all sizes that use AI in their businesses, and is intended to be relevant to all functions within those organisations; although it references Singapore's context, it aims to be globally relevant (p.8).

It addresses risks posed to FIs by the use of AI in their value chain – their business, vendors, and service providers such as contractors or consultants – and does NOT consider risks posed by the use of AI by unrelated parties or external malicious actors (p.8).
It covers all types of AI, including traditional AI, Gen AI, and Agentic AI (p.8).

It supplements and functions in tandem with existing non-AI-specific risk management practices (technology risk, cybersecurity, risk management); these are referred to where relevant but not replicated (p.8).

It describes only considerations unique or additional to AI governance and risk management, and does not duplicate or replace existing industry frameworks and good practices that are not AI-specific (p.11).
Based on principles of proportionality to risk and of relevance: not all practices will be feasible for all AI use cases, and FIs determine in context how to apply them (p.11).

The ten ABS 'top risks' were drawn from the MindForge Phase 1 AI risk taxonomy (updated version in Appendix B of the Operationalisation Handbook) via the ABS Handbook on Generative AI Guardrails in Banking; FIs should also continue to consider new, emerging, or diminished AI-specific risks (pp.8-9).

The Handbook builds on the FEAT Principles (2018) and the Veritas methodology, going beyond them by addressing enterprise governance, viewing AI use cases holistically rather than at model level, and considering a wider range of risks (seven risk dimensions in Appendix B) (p.12).
It is intended to accompany and support implementation of the proposed MAS Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence Risk Management; mapping in Appendix D (p.12).

'AI use cases' is the basic unit of AI governance and risk management, understood to include associated AI systems and models; FIs may choose their own basic unit so long as they effectively consider the relationship between models, systems, and use cases (p.16).
Terms such as Responsible AI, Trustworthy AI, and AI Safety are treated as referring to a broadly similar set of considerations and activities as 'AI governance and risk management' (p.14).

tiers.definition: One of the three tiers in the commonly used tiered approach ('Low', 'Medium', or 'High'). In the illustrative scoring method, a total of 0-4 points is Low Risk; in the flowchart method, a use case that is not credit/investment-related, not customer-service-related, and has risk-weighted materiality under $500k is Low Risk. An example of a use case with low residual risk materiality is an AI knowledge management chatbot interacting only with employees on an internal network on non-critical tasks.
tiers.governance_implications: Lower-risk materiality use cases receive less depth and autonomy of AI-specific review: FIs can use simple review questionnaires and review metric calculations completed by Builders rather than conducting them again; a peer review may suffice. Human-in-the-loop moderation could be applied on a sampling basis. For Gen AI, review can focus on conceptual soundness of grounding prompts/few-shot examples and on outcomes and sensitivity analysis.

source.quote: Risk materiality is often measured in a tiered approach, classified as "Low", "Medium", or "High".

tiers.definition: Middle tier in the tiered approach. In the illustrative scoring method a total of 5-9 points is Medium Risk. Examples of medium residual risk materiality include automated client sentiment analysis for relationship management, personal finance tools providing spending analysis and recommendations, or claims automation with human-in-the-loop oversight that avoids direct interactions between the AI system and the end customer.
tiers.governance_implications: Intermediate depth/autonomy of review; in the illustrative control library, some controls are applied at 'Medium - High Risk' (e.g. a Gen AI hallucination/fabrication/confabulation control).

source.quote: Examples of AI use cases with a medium residual risk materiality could be automated client sentiment analysis for relationship management

tiers.definition: Highest tier in the tiered approach. In the illustrative scoring method a total of 10+ points is High Risk; in the flowchart method, controlling credit or investment decisions (or providing material inputs to them) yields High Risk. An example of high residual risk materiality is a credit underwriting system that, based on personal information about customers, makes key decisions about that customer's creditworthiness.
tiers.governance_implications: Greater depth and autonomy of AI-specific review: FIs might require more detailed inputs from Builders, with reviewers rigorously verifying submissions, gathering information themselves and performing their own tests and calculations; independent reviewers such as an internal audit function or an external reviewer can be designated. Human-in-the-loop moderation may be applied more frequently or made mandatory for all outputs. Some controls apply at 'High Risk Only'. Post-deployment reviews are more frequent/deeper. For Gen AI, more extensive input/output controls (filtering, pseudonymisation) are typically in place and review focuses on their correct functioning.

source.quote: An example of an AI use case with high residual risk materiality could be a credit underwriting system

materiality.tiering_method: The handbook does not prescribe a single combination rule; each FI is responsible for determining criteria and establishing discrete tiers, with tiers explicitly defined and unambiguous so they can be consistently applied across the FI. It names two common approaches that can also be combined: the flowchart method (Use Case Owners answer straightforward, binary questions about the use case and its design in a sequence, which routes to a tier — effectively a highest-wins sequential triage) and the scoring method (developers complete a full questionnaire, with responses resulting in numerical scores corresponding to tiers, e.g. 0-4 Low, 5-9 Medium, 10+ High, with some items scoring cumulatively). The illustrative criteria in Figure 2.4.2 are simplified and not meant to represent a real assessment. Where assessments produce disagreements, FIs can designate a final authority to resolve differences or escalations.
materiality.residual_risk_logic: Residual risk materiality is assessed after controls and guardrails have been implemented (typically at the end of build/onboarding and prior to deployment), by qualitatively and/or quantitatively assessing the use case's behaviour in a setting representative of its intended real use with all guardrails applied. FIs define a methodology for considering both the results of this assessment and the inherent risk materiality to assign a tier of residual risk materiality. Assessment results can be rated against the use case's KPIs as meeting minimal acceptance thresholds, exceeding them, or meeting a high, industry-leading standard of performance; use cases that fail to meet minimums do not proceed. Figure 2.4.3 gives a notional matrix: a low inherent risk use case stays Low Risk regardless of evaluation result; a medium inherent use case is Medium at 'Min.' and 'Exceeds Min.' but Low at 'Best Practice'; a high inherent use case remains High Risk at 'Min.' and 'Exceeds Min.' and only becomes 'Medium Risk/High Risk' at best practice (depending on the FI's risk tiers and risk tolerance, some use cases may always have a high residual risk). Achieving minimum evaluation results never elevates a low inherent-risk use case to overall 'high'. FIs may iteratively add controls and re-assess residual risk as many times as required, and residual risk materiality can be periodically re-assessed post-deployment as part of AI-specific review. The approach is notional and depends on each FI's risk tolerance, assessment methodology, and tier definitions.
agentic_or_genai_factors: Table 2.4.1: for Gen AI, the broad range of business applications increases the importance of thoroughly assessing each context of use rather than just the model's risks; complexity is generally higher.

Table 2.4.1: for Agentic AI, the large number of broad, complex business uses and complex interactions between numerous traditional AI and Gen AI models makes it essential to consider broader use case factors when assessing risk; complexity and operational independence are both generally higher.

Complexity of the AI in use criterion explicitly cites complex architectures (e.g. LLMs) and multiple models in concert (e.g. agentic AI) as complexity drivers that limit interpretability or predictability.
Figure 2.4.5 and surrounding text: depth of AI-specific review increases with both risk materiality and the degree of operational autonomy.

Gen AI 'use case' validation focus areas: fit for purpose, Gen AI-specific risks (hallucinations, toxicity, offensive content), and risk-based guardrails (adversarial testing, output filtering, human oversight).

Gen AI review challenges: large proprietary training datasets precluding complete data quality checks, deep/complex architectures where existing explainability techniques are insufficient, and SaaS delivery limiting direct access — warranting compensatory testing (simulation, scenario, sensitivity testing, red teaming) and third-party disclosures like 'AI cards'.

Control library illustration: red-teaming is relevant to Gen AI but less so to conventional analytics models; a hallucination/fabrication/confabulation control applies to Gen AI at Medium - High Risk.

risks.name: Lack of AI risk awareness
risks.description: Insufficient education or reskilling resulting in undertrained resources lacking awareness of the unique risks involved with Gen AI. Also, over-reliance on Gen AI can lead to an erroneous, biased, or misleading outputs being accepted without adequate scrutiny. The disposition of Gen AI to produce outputs that are not easily interpretable or verifiable amplifies this risk. This reliance can compromise the quality and integrity of decision-making processes, as well as erode trust in institutional operations.
risks.ai_specific_elements: AI presents unique risks to an FI and, especially in the case of Gen AI, may directly impact more employees. The potential for misuse when employees are not aware of the specific risks of AI is an enhanced risk.

oversight_modes.definition: Where an employee retains full control of the use case and either approves or executes actions at crucial points in operation. This may take the form of an employee reviewing AI-generated customer service emails before approving them for sending, or an AI advisor that suggests actions to a relationship manager.
oversight_modes.when_appropriate: The handbook does not specify a distinct risk trigger for this mode; it indicates the choice of oversight form is decided at the use case design stage based on the use case's inherent risk materiality, its intended modality, and the feasibility of human oversight. Examples given are review of AI-generated customer service emails before sending and an AI advisor suggesting actions to a relationship manager.

source.quote: Human in the Loop: Where an employee retains full control of the use case and either approves or executes actions at crucial points in operation

oversight_modes.definition: The AI use case produces outputs or actions where an employee has the option to modify or overrule its outputs or intervene in its operations but is not required to take any action in the course of normal operation. This includes situations where an AI use case escalates errors or anomalies to an employee for review, or where an employee reviews some or all outputs after the fact.
oversight_modes.when_appropriate: Suitable where errors or anomalies are escalated to an employee for review or where outputs are reviewed after the fact; post-event monitoring or exception handling may be used where real-time oversight is infeasible (e.g. high-volume/high-throughput AI such as autonomous chatbots or fraud detection engines). Where designed in, it is operationalised post-deployment via sampling methodologies (targeted high-frequency review for higher-risk use cases, lower-frequency review for lower-risk use cases, and threshold-based review suitable for all use cases), proportionate to risk materiality and operational feasibility.

source.quote: Human over the Loop: The AI use case produces outputs or actions where an employee has the option to modify or overrule its outputs

oversight_modes.definition: The AI use case produces outputs without direct involvement from an employee, such as in an autonomous chatbot. While this means that the AI can take actions autonomously, it does not imply the absence of other forms of oversight, such as post-deployment testing, monitoring, and review.
oversight_modes.when_appropriate: Appropriate where human oversight may not be suitable or feasible, such as AI handling high volumes of tasks or high throughput (e.g. autonomous chatbots or fraud detection engines), where real-time human oversight may not be feasible; other forms of oversight such as post-deployment testing, monitoring, and review still apply.

source.quote: Human out of the Loop: The AI use case produces outputs without direct involvement from an employee

sampling_methodologies.name: Targeted High-Frequency Review
sampling_methodologies.description: High-frequency reviews are conducted more frequently, using a representative sample of outputs. This ensures that outputs meet required standards and allows the use case team to take remediation action quickly if issues occur.
sampling_methodologies.when_to_use: Higher-risk use cases (e.g. AI-generated customer interactions for financial advice).

source.quote: High-frequency reviews are conducted more frequently, using a representative sample of outputs.

sampling_methodologies.name: Lower-Frequency Review
sampling_methodologies.description: Human reviews can be done less frequently on a representative sample of the AI's output if the use-case has a lower risk materiality. This helps to reduce unnecessary governance effort.
sampling_methodologies.when_to_use: Lower-risk use cases (e.g. internal knowledge assistants).

source.quote: Human reviews can be done less frequently on a representative sample of the AI's output

sampling_methodologies.name: Threshold-Based Review
sampling_methodologies.description: Threshold-based reviews do not involve human oversight in the course of normal operation, but may trigger a human review when certain conditions are met (such as a breach of risk metric thresholds).
sampling_methodologies.when_to_use: Suitable for all use cases regardless of risk materiality.

source.quote: Threshold-based reviews do not involve human oversight in the course of normal operation

monitoring_practices.description: A plan defined before deployment documenting key AI risk-related performance metrics and thresholds, how they will be tracked, the frequency of monitoring (calibrated to risk materiality), and the escalation process if thresholds are exceeded.

source.quote: Define a post-deployment monitoring plan performance metrics and thresholds to be tracked as part of the monitoring process

monitoring_practices.description: For higher risk materiality use cases, tracking near misses, early warnings and cases where metrics approach but do not surpass thresholds, using lower thresholds to activate "near miss" indications so issues are rectified before becoming serious.

monitoring_practices.control: Designated monitoring accountabilities and operational ownership

monitoring_practices.control: ITSM Incident and Problem Management integration

monitoring_practices.control: Ongoing monitoring and reporting of AI risk, performance and guardrail metrics

monitoring_practices.description: A common visualisation technique for ongoing AI monitoring results, especially for executive audiences, communicating breaches, near misses and performance within tolerances.

monitoring_practices.control: Logging of monitoring results, incidents and escalations

monitoring_practices.control: Data quality, drift and third-party data monitoring
monitoring_practices.description: Ongoing monitoring of input and training data quality, drift and risk indicators at a frequency and depth proportionate to risk materiality, including third-party dataset characteristics such as consent validity, usage requirements and statistical properties, with mitigation (e.g. retraining) when indicators fall outside thresholds.

source.quote: Monitor data quality, drift, and risk indicators at a frequency and depth proportionate to the use case's risk materiality.

monitoring_practices.description: Periodic self-checks by the use case team for changes in risk materiality, scope of usage and key risks, calibrated in depth and frequency to risk materiality; may include simulation testing, adversarial testing, or calculation of metrics/benchmarks for material use cases.

monitoring_practices.description: Periodic and proportionate repetition of AI-specific reviews after deployment to assess emerging risks such as data drift or repurposing for unapproved uses, triggered by risk materiality, major model/system changes, KPI breaches, stakeholder feedback or external risk factors.

monitoring_practices.description: Implementing a proportionate degree of human oversight post-deployment, with overseers enabled with tools, training, transparency and explainability measures, and documentation of issues identified or interventions taken; sampling methodology per Table 3.5.1.

monitoring_practices.control: End user feedback, enquiry and review channels
monitoring_practices.description: Avenues such as feedback or contact forms, online portals, hotlines or in-branch support for users to seek support, raise concerns, contest outcomes and request human review; simple ratings (thumbs up/down) quantified as metrics triggering alerts when negative feedback exceeds a threshold or trend.

monitoring_practices.control: Security monitoring of unstructured inputs/outputs (input and output filtering)

monitoring_practices.description: Enhanced risk management for frequently retrained (dynamic) AI, including justifications for automatic updates, enhanced data quality checks, drift detection and more stringent performance monitoring with tighter notification thresholds.

source.quote: enhanced data quality checks, drift detection, and more stringent performance monitoring with tighter notification thresholds

monitoring_practices.control: Compensating monitoring where third-party change notification is absent
monitoring_practices.description: Where a use case containing third-party AI is deployed without assurance of sufficient change notification, controls such as increased frequency of reviews or an enhanced level of post-deployment monitoring are considered.

source.quote: an increased frequency of reviews or an enhanced level of post-deployment monitoring, to mitigate the risks

interruption_controls.description: A safeguard to deactivate the AI use case where it breaches risk thresholds or exhibits undesirable behaviour, ensuring no further harm while the issue is investigated; FIs can consider testing it prior to deployment.

interruption_controls.control: Rollback to a previous stable version

interruption_controls.description: Applying existing contingency planning measures for third party software, proportionately planning for service interruptions, performance degradations, or support discontinuation of third party AI products/services.

source.quote: planning for service interruptions, performance degradations, or support discontinuation

interruption_controls.description: The monitoring plan specifies the escalation process if metric thresholds are exceeded, with employees/functions having sufficient authority to execute the contingencies defined in the monitoring plan.

interruption_controls.control: Phased rollout failure criteria triggering deactivation
interruption_controls.description: Clear success and failure criteria for each phase of a phased rollout, where failure criteria could trigger deactivation; scope, features, user numbers and phase duration are strictly limited with additional monitoring in place.

source.quote: Clear success and failure criteria (the latter of which could trigger deactivation) for each phase

interruption_controls.control: Incident response mechanisms (roll-backs and kill switches)
interruption_controls.description: Following the incident and problem management plan and implementing response mechanisms such as model retraining, adjustments, redevelopment, rolling back to a previous version of the model, or activating a kill switch when incidents or guardrail failures are identified.

interruption_controls.control: Escalation of changes by the use case team

source.quote: when automated monitoring detects a potential breach, human review can be triggered to determine the seriousness

interruption_controls.control: Escalation to a human agent / human recourse
interruption_controls.description: End users can be connected to a human agent where the AI (e.g. a chatbot) cannot address their needs, and impacted parties are given human recourse, remediation, appeal, or human review of a decision.

source.quote: a chatbot may provide an option to connect the user to a human agent if it is unable to address the user's needs

interruption_controls.description: Safeguards that flag and block inappropriate, confidential, or adversarial inputs or outputs to mitigate detected security threats such as prompt injection during system usage.

source.quote: flagging and blocking inappropriate, confidential, or adversarial inputs or outputs

interruption_controls.description: Negative user feedback tracked as a metric triggers alerts when it exceeds a threshold or trend; substantiated feedback or escalations are treated as AI risk events, issues or incidents that trigger review processes and changes to the use case.

source.quote: triggering alerts when the proportion of negative feedback increases beyond a threshold or trend

interruption_controls.control: Go/no-go checkpoint and use case rejection (tollgates)

source.quote: individual risk type owners evaluate AI-relevant risks within their areas, recommend mitigation strategies as needed, or reject a given use case

monitoring.selection_guidance: The handbook (Subsection 3.1, Consideration 7, Practice 4, printed page 70) says FIs typically decide at the use case design stage how best to integrate human oversight, basing the decision on the use case's inherent risk materiality, its intended modality, and the feasibility of human oversight. Human oversight complements monitoring by integrating human judgement, but may not be suitable for all use cases: for AI handling high volumes of tasks or high throughput (e.g. autonomous chatbots, fraud detection engines), real-time oversight may not be feasible and may instead take the form of post-event monitoring or exception handling. FIs can make an informed decision during design, and revisit it throughout the lifecycle, balancing operational considerations with risk. The three forms are drawn from the IMDA/PDPC Model AI Governance Framework. It is important to clearly define and document roles, responsibilities and escalations, and to ensure the employees involved have sufficient competencies and authority; FIs may have risk-related controls specifying the conditions under which human oversight of AI is expected. Subsection 3.5, Practice 5 (printed page 102) adds that the appropriate degree of oversight is defined at the design stage and reaffirmed throughout the lifecycle based on technical and operational feasibility and risk materiality, and that human-over-the-loop review should be operationalised with an appropriate sampling methodology (see Table 3.5.1, printed page 103).

metrics.name: Average Absolute Odds Difference (AAOD)
metrics.definition: AAOD combines differences in false positive and true positive rates across two groups (a and b) to provide a comprehensive view of classification disparities.
metrics.formula: 0.5 x (|FPRa - FPRb| + |TPRa - TPRb|) Where FPR is False Positive Rate and TPR is True Positive Rate.

source.quote: AAOD combines differences in false positive and true positive rates across two groups (a and b)

metrics.name: Disparate Impact Ratio (DIR)
metrics.definition: DIR measures the ratio of favourable outcome probabilities between groups, aligning with legal frameworks like the "80% rule" in US employment law (80% rule helps employers and EEOC determine if a selection process has a disproportionate negative impact on protected groups).
metrics.formula: P(Y=1|A=0) / P(Y=1|A=1) Where Y is an outcome and A is a sensitive variable.

source.quote: DIR measures the ratio of favourable outcome probabilities between groups, aligning with legal frameworks like the "80% rule"

metrics.name: Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD)
metrics.definition: EOD focuses on equality of opportunity by measuring the ratio of differences in true positive rates across groups.
metrics.formula: P(Y=1|Y*=1, A=0) - P(Y=1|Y*=1, A=1) Where Y is an outcome, Y* is the true outcome, and A is a sensitive variable.

source.quote: EOD focuses on equality of opportunity by measuring the ratio of differences in true positive rates across groups.

metrics.name: LLM-as-a-judge bias scoring
metrics.definition: LLM bias can be assessed using an LLM "as a judge", with frameworks provided by several open-source resources. Typically, the "judge" LLM is given a set of instructions for evaluating a corpus of outputs from the LLM targeted for evaluation. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation can output a score for bias (using a technique like G-Eval), but depending on the choice of judge, LLM-generated scores can display arbitrariness. Alternative approaches include QAG scores or other methods that use binary classification to rate outputs as either "biased" or "not biased", taking the proportion of biased outputs as a score.
metrics.formula: (Biased outputs / Total outputs) x 100%

source.quote: LLM bias can be assessed using an LLM "as a judge", with frameworks provided by several open-source resources.

metrics.name: Separation
metrics.definition: Separation measures the ratio of an outcome given a sensitive attribute to the probability of that outcome overall. A separation value closer to 1 indicates that predictions are less influenced by the sensitive variable.
metrics.formula: P(Y=1|A=1) / P(Y=1) Where Y is an outcome and A is a sensitive attribute.

source.quote: Separation measures the ratio of an outcome given a sensitive attribute to the probability of that outcome overall.

metrics.name: Socio-cultural bias
metrics.definition: Socio-cultural bias is when an LLM's behaviour varies in undesired ways when the context of customer interactions changes (e.g. different tone, decisions due to language/age/race/religion of customer, including indirect information through name). Though underlying data does not exhibit inherent bias, the Gen AI tooling may. It is typically measured with conversation flows with different customer context, including language, customer name, and background. Socio-cultural bias can be measured as a proportion of biased outputs over total outputs or using measures of semantic distance like cosine similarity.

source.quote: Socio-cultural bias is when an LLM's behaviour varies in undesired ways when the context of customer interactions changes

metrics.name: Statistical Parity Difference (SPD)
metrics.definition: SPD measures demographic parity by comparing the probability of a positive outcome between two groups.
metrics.formula: P(Y=1|A=0) - P(Y=1|A=1) Where Y is an outcome and A is a sensitive variable.

source.quote: SPD measures demographic parity by comparing the probability of a positive outcome between two groups.

metrics.name: Sufficiency
metrics.definition: Sufficiency measures disparities in outcomes given a sensitive attribute. A sufficiency value closer to 1 indicates that the outcome is not likely to be influenced by the sensitive variable.
metrics.formula: P(Y) / P(Y|A) Where Y is an outcome and A is a sensitive variable.

source.quote: Sufficiency measures disparities in outcomes given a sensitive attribute.

metrics.name: Toxicity Score
metrics.definition: Similar to other metrics on bias, the toxicity score is the proportion of toxic outputs. Toxicity can be quantified using an LLM as a judge, by regex matching, or by semantic scoring.
metrics.formula: (Number of toxic opinions / Total number of opinions extracted) x 100%

source.quote: the toxicity score is the proportion of toxic outputs. Toxicity can be quantified using an LLM as a judge

metrics.name: Compliance Consistency Score (CCS)
metrics.definition: A normalised score (0 to 1) reflecting the overall quality and consistency of policy adherence.

source.quote: A normalised score (0 to 1) reflecting the overall quality and consistency of policy adherence.

metrics.name: Policy Override Frequency (POF)
metrics.definition: A measure of the extent to which policies are adhered to.
metrics.formula: (Number of policy deviation instances / Total number of prompts) x 100%

source.quote: A measure of the extent to which policies are adhered to. It is given by:

metrics.name: Feature attribution
metrics.definition: Measures the change in contribution of features to a model's prediction compared to a baseline. Common measures for doing so include: LIME value (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations); SHAP value (SHapley Additive exPlanations)

source.quote: Measures the change in contribution of features to a model's prediction compared to a baseline.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: Accuracy measures the overall correctness of predictions across all classes.
metrics.formula: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) Where TP is True Positives, TN is True Negatives, FP is False Positives, and FN is False Negatives.

source.quote: Accuracy measures the overall correctness of predictions across all classes.

metrics.name: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy)
metrics.definition: A longstanding metric for quantifying the similarity of translated text to a translation by a human expert; it is useful for quantifying a model or system's translation accuracy. BLEU can be calculated on a body of customised domain-specific translations or on a benchmark reference set of translated pairs. METEOR is an industry alternative to BLEU that aims to account for variances like word order.

source.quote: A longstanding metric for quantifying the similarity of translated text to a translation by a human expert

metrics.name: Consistency check
metrics.definition: Hallucinated facts in LLM-generated responses are less likely to be repeated between responses than facts that are supported by facts. With this fact in mind it is possible to perform a "zero-resource" check – that is, without requiring consultation of additional sources. A consistency check involves assessing each sentence of an output against several other sample outputs generated from the same prompt; assessment typically involves a similarity metric like BERTScore. A lower average similarity to sentences in the other samples indicates a higher likelihood of hallucination.

source.quote: Hallucinated facts in LLM-generated responses are less likely to be repeated between responses

metrics.name: F1 Score
metrics.definition: F1 Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balanced measure when classes are imbalanced.
metrics.formula: 2 x (Precision x Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

source.quote: F1 Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balanced measure when classes are imbalanced.

metrics.name: Input feature data drift
metrics.definition: Measures the distribution of input feature values compared to a baseline data distribution. Categorical: Boolean, string, L-Infinity, Jensen Shannon Divergence. Numerical: Float, integer, Jensen Shannon Divergence

source.quote: Measures the distribution of input feature values compared to a baseline data distribution.

metrics.name: Output prediction data drift
metrics.definition: Measures the model's predicted data distribution compared to a baseline data distribution. Categorical: Boolean, string, L-Infinity, Jensen Shannon Divergence. Numerical: float, integer, Jensen Shannon Divergence

source.quote: Measures the model's predicted data distribution compared to a baseline data distribution.

metrics.name: Precision
metrics.definition: Precision measures the proportion of positive identifications that were correct.
metrics.formula: TP / (TP + FP) Where TP is True Positives, FP is False Positives.

source.quote: Precision measures the proportion of positive identifications that were correct.

metrics.name: Prediction error percentage
metrics.definition: A high error rate might indicate an issue with the model or with the requests to the model.
metrics.formula: (Incorrect Predictions / Total Predictions) x100%

source.quote: A high error rate might indicate an issue with the model or with the requests to the model.

metrics.name: Recall
metrics.definition: Recall (also called sensitivity) measures the proportion of actual positives that were correctly identified.
metrics.formula: TP / (TP + FN) Where TP is True Positives, FN is False Negatives

source.quote: Recall (also called sensitivity) measures the proportion of actual positives that were correctly identified.

metrics.name: Relevance to prompt
metrics.definition: The cosine distance or BERTScore of the prompt to the generated output. This gives an indication of how relevant the response is to the prompt and can be useful in detecting off-topic outputs. The number or proportion of outputs with a low relevance can also be tracked as a metric.

source.quote: The cosine distance or BERTScore of the prompt to the generated output.

metrics.name: SARI (System output Against References and against the Input sentence)
metrics.definition: A longstanding metric for quantifying the similarity between a simplified/summarised output and a source text. SARI can be calculated on a body of customised domain-specific summarisations or on a benchmark reference set of texts and reference summarisations.

source.quote: A longstanding metric for quantifying the similarity between a simplified/summarised output and a source text.

metrics.name: Topic and task adherence
metrics.definition: A metric for checking if an LLM system stays on topic. This risk metric can also be used to detect if corporate Gen AI tools are used for personal tasks provided that those tools are effective in refusing off-topic prompts.
metrics.formula: (Prompts Refused / Total Prompts) x100%

source.quote: A metric for checking if an LLM system stays on topic.

metrics.name: Injection Similarity
metrics.definition: Prompt injection attempts can be detected by calculating semantic similarity measures – like cosine distance – for any given prompt against a library of templates of known prompt injection or jailbreak formats. There are several open-source resources that catalogue known prompt injection attempts; the currency of these templates is important as prompt injection formats continue to evolve. The number of prompts that are similar to a known injection format (cosine similarity >0.85 is considered likely to be harmful, and >0.5 may merit investigation) can be tracked as a metric.

source.quote: Prompt injection attempts can be detected by calculating semantic similarity measures – like cosine distance

metrics.name: Injection Success Rate (ISR)
metrics.definition: A score indicating the success, in either a controlled environment or in production, of attempts to inject adversarial prompts into the system.
metrics.formula: (Number of successful injection attempts / Total number of injection attempts) x 100%

source.quote: A score indicating the success, in either a controlled environment or in production, of attempts to inject adversarial prompts

metrics.name: PII Detection Rate
metrics.definition: The outputs of an LLM can be assessed for the presence of PII, with the proportion of outputs containing PII quantified in the aggregate or by PII type. A range of PII detectors, both open-source and proprietary, exist in the market today. These may either use an LLM or regex matching (or a combination of the two) to detect data resembles PII categories like names, addresses, phone numbers, password, or credentials.
metrics.formula: (Prompts containing PII / Total number of prompts) x 100%

source.quote: The outputs of an LLM can be assessed for the presence of PII

metrics.name: Prompt Refusal
metrics.definition: The number or proportion of prompts that are rejected by a Gen AI system's guardrails can be detected by an LLM judge or regex expression and tracked as a metric. This can indicate both the effectiveness of the FI's guardrails, by tracking that they continue to reject prompts at a sustained rate, and can serve as an indicator of a potential attack on the system.
metrics.formula: (Prompts rejected / Total number of prompts) x 100%

source.quote: The number or proportion of prompts that are rejected by a Gen AI system's guardrails

metrics.name: Prompt Sanitisation Rate (PSR)
metrics.definition: This metric is a complement to ISR and indicates the success rate of guardrails against prompt injection.
metrics.formula: (Number of successfully neutralised injection attempts / Total detected injection attempts) x 100%

source.quote: This metric is a complement to ISR and indicates the success rate of guardrails against prompt injection.

metrics.name: Red-teaming attempts
metrics.definition: Red-teaming attempts are intentional attempts to get LLMs to leak data, including system prompts, or output potentially harmful and embarrassing content. It is typically used with benchmark prompt injection datasets or long context prompt attacks. Specifically for our region, we can include multilingual prompts and conversations.
metrics.formula: (Successful attacks / Total attacks) x 100%

source.quote: Red-teaming attempts are intentional attempts to get LLMs to leak data, including system prompts

metrics.name: Total Injection Vulnerability Score (TIVS)
metrics.definition: A composite metric incorporating the above (and other) measurements to provide a comprehensive view of prompt injection vulnerability. Each organisation can select the measurements for calculating TIVS in their context.

source.quote: A composite metric incorporating the above (and other) measurements to provide a comprehensive view of prompt injection vulnerability.

metrics.name: Accelerator average duty cycle.
metrics.definition: The average fraction of time over the past sample period during which one or more accelerators were actively processing.

source.quote: The average fraction of time over the past sample period during which one or more accelerators were actively processing.

metrics.name: Accelerator memory usage
metrics.definition: The amount of memory allocated by the deployed model replica.

source.quote: The amount of memory allocated by the deployed model replica.

metrics.name: CPU utilisation
metrics.definition: The fraction of CPU allocated by the feature store and currently in use by online storage. This number can exceed 100% if the online serving storage is overloaded.

source.quote: The fraction of CPU allocated by the feature store and currently in use by online storage.

metrics.name: CPU utilisation – hottest node
metrics.definition: The CPU load for the hottest node in a feature store's online storage.

source.quote: The CPU load for the hottest node in a feature store's online storage.

metrics.name: Latency
metrics.definition: The total time that an online serving or streaming ingestion request spends in the service.

source.quote: The total time that an online serving or streaming ingestion request spends in the service.

metrics.name: Memory usage
metrics.definition: The amount of memory allocated by the deployed model replica and currently in use.

source.quote: The amount of memory allocated by the deployed model replica and currently in use.

metrics.name: Model latency
metrics.definition: The time spent performing computation.

source.quote: Model latency The time spent performing computation.

metrics.name: Network bytes received
metrics.definition: The number of bytes received over the network by the deployed model replica.

source.quote: The number of bytes received over the network by the deployed model replica.

metrics.name: Network bytes sent
metrics.definition: The number of bytes sent over the network by the deployed model replica.

source.quote: The number of bytes sent over the network by the deployed model replica.

metrics.name: Node count
metrics.definition: The number of online serving nodes for a feature store.

source.quote: Node count The number of online serving nodes for a feature store.

metrics.name: Offline storage write for streaming write
metrics.definition: The number of streaming write requests processed for the offline storage.

source.quote: The number of streaming write requests processed for the offline storage.

metrics.name: Online serving throughput
metrics.definition: The throughput for online serving requests in MB/s.

source.quote: The throughput for online serving requests in MB/s.

metrics.name: Overhead latency
metrics.definition: The total time spent processing a request, outside of computation.

source.quote: The total time spent processing a request, outside of computation.

metrics.name: Predictions per second
metrics.definition: The number of predictions per second across both online and batch predictions.

source.quote: The number of predictions per second across both online and batch predictions.

metrics.name: Queries per second
metrics.definition: The number of online serving or streaming ingestion queries that a feature store handles.

source.quote: The number of online serving or streaming ingestion queries that a feature store handles.

metrics.name: Replica count
metrics.definition: The number of active replicas used by the deployed model.

source.quote: The number of active replicas used by the deployed model.

metrics.name: Replica target
metrics.definition: The number of active replicas required for the deployed model.

source.quote: The number of active replicas required for the deployed model.

metrics.name: Request size
metrics.definition: The request size by entity type in a feature store.

source.quote: The request size by entity type in a feature store.

metrics.name: Streaming write to offline storage delay time
metrics.definition: The time elapsed (in seconds) between calling the write API and writing to the offline storage.

source.quote: The time elapsed (in seconds) between calling the write API and writing to the offline storage.

metrics.name: Total latency duration
metrics.definition: The total time that a request spends in the service, which is the model latency plus the overhead latency.

source.quote: The total time that a request spends in the service, which is the model latency plus the overhead latency.

metrics.name: Total offline storage
metrics.definition: Amount of data stored in the feature store's offline storage.

source.quote: Amount of data stored in the feature store's offline storage.

metrics.name: Total online storage
metrics.definition: Amount of data stored in the feature store's online storage.

source.quote: Amount of data stored in the feature store's online storage.

guardrails.name: Algorithm re-selection
guardrails.description: The practice of selecting a different training algorithm that performs better, ceteris paribus, on fairness criteria.

source.quote: The practice of selecting a different training algorithm that performs better, ceteris paribus, on fairness criteria.

guardrails.name: Decision threshold adjustment
guardrails.description: Adjustment of the decision thresholds for different groups to ensure that each group receives fair treatment.

source.quote: Adjustment of the decision thresholds for different groups to ensure that each group receives fair treatment.

guardrails.name: Hyperparameter tuning
guardrails.description: The practice of modifying system hyperparameters. Different types of AI have a wide variety in such parameters. In Gen AI applications that involve Large Language Models, common hyperparameters are temperature, which represents a model's "creativity"; k, which represents the range of possible responses; and p, which represents the likelihood of choosing less-likely responses. In applications where random fairness-violating responses are generated, these three values can each be reduced.

source.quote: common hyperparameters are temperature, which represents a model's "creativity"

guardrails.name: Input/output filtering
guardrails.description: The addition of filters to a Gen AI use case to detect biased or toxic content. Input filtering involves checking prompts for toxic language (often using regex matching or agentic monitoring), checking if they are on topic, or assessing whether they can induce the model to behave inappropriately. Output filtering involves checking a model's outputs to determine whether it contains toxicity (often using a word list or sentiment measure), is unrepresentative, or otherwise contains content which meets harm thresholds (often using an agentic architecture).

source.quote: The addition of filters to a Gen AI use case to detect biased or toxic content.

guardrails.name: In-processing techniques
guardrails.description: Manual adjustments to a model's loss function, the addition of variables, or the use of other algorithms that change the model or its decision-making process to prioritise fairness. These include adversarial debiasing, reductions grid search, automatic hyperparameter tuning, or the addition of fairness regularisers to a regression.

source.quote: These include adversarial debiasing, reductions grid search, automatic hyperparameter tuning

guardrails.name: Model customisation
guardrails.description: Model customisation in pretrained models, especially Gen AI, refers to fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Fine-tuning adds layers to the model based on data, such as additional data representing individuals or groups who may be discriminated against. Reinforcement learning uses human review to reward or punish the model for harmful outputs, modifying the model's parameters towards responses that meet fairness criteria.

source.quote: Model customisation in pretrained models, especially Gen AI, refers to fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

guardrails.name: Model separation
guardrails.description: The demarcation of different models for handling different types of uses, such as by splitting customers into two types and training models to address each distinctly. This is useful for cases where customer types are meaningfully distinct and a single model is less effective at fairly treating each.

source.quote: The demarcation of different models for handling different types of uses

guardrails.name: Post-processing techniques
guardrails.description: The modification of model outputs to improve AI performance on fairness characteristics. These include output adjustment to generate equal odds for different groups or constrained balanced accuracy for supervised learning.

source.quote: The modification of model outputs to improve AI performance on fairness characteristics.

guardrails.name: Prompt design
guardrails.description: The addition of instructions to user prompts. These can include instructions to represent groups fairly, reject requests to create discriminatory content, or instructions to include different individuals or groups in outputs.

source.quote: The addition of instructions to user prompts. These can include instructions to represent groups fairly

guardrails.name: Algorithm selection for power efficiency
guardrails.description: AI training algorithms can have significantly different power requirements for certain types of tasks. Choosing the right algorithm for a specific task – and balancing both performance and efficiency – is an important part of the build process that can have significant impacts on the power consumption and environmental impact of the training or fine-tuning process.

source.quote: AI training algorithms can have significantly different power requirements for certain types of tasks.

guardrails.name: Conduct an ethical design assessment in onboarding
guardrails.description: When onboarding systems or models, FIs can assess the extent to which their design, functioning, and use supports enterprise values and ethical principles. Third-party vendors can provide information on the ethical principles used in the system's design, and these can be assessed against the FI's own ethics.

source.quote: When onboarding systems or models, FIs can assess the extent to which their design, functioning, and use supports enterprise values

guardrails.name: Test prioritisation
guardrails.description: FIs can prioritise the sequence of tests that are performed on an AI to improve the efficiency of the testing process, reduce the number of re-training runs that need to be performed, and potentially reduce the number of tests that need to be performed. Carefully sequencing, de-duplicating, and triaging tests, typically by performing the most rigorous and comprehensive tests first, can minimise the need for power-intensive re-testing and re-training of an AI.

source.quote: FIs can prioritise the sequence of tests that are performed on an AI to improve the efficiency

guardrails.name: Content Moderation
guardrails.description: FIs can assess the outputs of a Gen AI system for ethical compliance before sharing them with the user. This assessment can take the form of deterministic rules, but is typically implemented using an LLM (for text outputs) which assesses whether the output violates the FI's policies or principles. Outputs that fail to pass can be re-generated or can result in an error message. This approach often uses the same techniques as "input/output filtering", which is included under "Fairness & Bias".

source.quote: FIs can assess the outputs of a Gen AI system for ethical compliance before sharing them with the user.

guardrails.name: Use of pre-trained models
guardrails.description: By leveraging pre-trained or pre-tuned AI models, FIs can limit or completely avoid the requirement to perform their own training or find-tuning activities, with potentially significant power savings as a consequence.

source.quote: By leveraging pre-trained or pre-tuned AI models, FIs can limit or completely avoid the requirement

guardrails.name: Chain-of-thought prompting
guardrails.description: LLMs can, through grounding or prompting, be induced to produce outputs in a stepwise fashion. This encourages the system to illustrate reasoning steps in generating an output and can significantly improve the explainability of those outputs by clarifying the assumptions underlying it; it has the side effect of also improving the accuracy of some kinds of outputs. Chain-of-thought prompting is an area of ongoing research and is known to have limitations.

source.quote: LLMs can, through grounding or prompting, be induced to produce outputs in a stepwise fashion.

guardrails.name: Confidence scoring
guardrails.description: There are a variety of measures of the degree to which an AI is "confident" in its outputs. Perplexity is a common measure of confidence for NLP and is especially useful in LLMs. Confidence levels can be used by builders to assess the usefulness and effectiveness of their AI, and AI outputs with low confidence scores can trigger different behaviours.

source.quote: Perplexity is a common measure of confidence for NLP and is especially useful in LLMs.

guardrails.name: Counterfactual explanations
guardrails.description: Counterfactual explanations test how AI might behave under different input conditions, creating a form of explainability by suggesting which features or factors may have contributed to an output. Builders can include counterfactual explainability techniques in use cases that they create, particularly in traditional AI.

source.quote: Counterfactual explanations test how AI might behave under different input conditions

guardrails.name: Inherent interpretability
guardrails.description: Some types of models, especially those with low dimensionality or that create outputs as a weighted sum of inputs (such as a linear regression), are inherently interpretable. Models built using decision trees, decision sets, or rule-based classifiers are also considered inherently interpretable. The selection of such a model significantly enhances explainability.

source.quote: Models built using decision trees, decision sets, or rule-based classifiers are also considered inherently interpretable.

guardrails.name: Interpretability constraints
guardrails.description: AI with interpretability constraints are systems whose characteristics have been modified to improve their interpretability, sometimes at the cost of a penalty to performance. Interpretability constraints include rule-based reasoning or measures to sparsify neural networks.

source.quote: AI with interpretability constraints are systems whose characteristics have been modified to improve their interpretability

guardrails.name: Post hoc interpretability techniques
guardrails.description: Post-hoc interpretability techniques support the analysis of black box models by attempting to assess how an output was created. These techniques vary in complexity and applicability to different model architectures. Such techniques consist of building surrogate models, generating Shapley values, or assessing deep learning models using gradient-based assessments.

source.quote: Post-hoc interpretability techniques support the analysis of black box models by attempting to assess how an output was created.

guardrails.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
guardrails.description: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture supplements an LLM with other components that provide it with sources on which to base its output. Some LLMs are capable of citing sources contextually in-line throughout an output, which provides a user with clear traceability to sources and provides an opportunity to validate the use of those sources. This can improve the explainability of use case outputs.

source.quote: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture supplements an LLM with other components that provide it with sources

guardrails.name: System prompt design
guardrails.description: The addition of instructions to user prompts. These can include instructions to reject prompts where the system cannot produce a satisfactory answer or where source data does not match the type of output desired.

source.quote: These can include instructions to reject prompts where the system cannot produce a satisfactory answer

guardrails.name: Programmable conversation controls
guardrails.description: Rule-based frameworks can be used to define explicit boundaries for multi-turn conversations, ensuring that outputs consistently remain within approved topics and organisational policies. Such rules can support the codification of compliance requirements as transparent, enforceable rules with clear logic.

source.quote: Rule-based frameworks can be used to define explicit boundaries for multi-turn conversations

guardrails.name: AI onboarding using domain data
guardrails.description: Testing that focuses on performance on domain data, such as by testing the AI against internal data or against a finance-specific benchmark, can provide assurance in cases where training data is not transparent.

source.quote: Testing that focuses on performance on domain data, such as by testing the AI against internal data

guardrails.name: Fine-tuning
guardrails.description: For AI models based on neural networks, fine-tuning is the additional of neural "layers" based on additional data without adjusting the underlying parameters. Fine-tuning is a resource-efficient method for adjusting system performance characteristics and introducing domain-specific data without fully retraining the model. It is particularly useful for preparing models for unexpected use or introducing a wider variety of data or circumstances. Common fine-tuning datasets include: • Fact-checking datasets, which consist of pairs of prompts and correct responses. • Negative examples, which suggest outputs that a model should avoid. • Domain data, which consists of data relevant to the FI's expected usage.

source.quote: Fine-tuning is a resource-efficient method for adjusting system performance characteristics and introducing domain-specific data

guardrails.name: Input filtering
guardrails.description: Gen AI use cases can be vulnerable to the ingestion of low-quality or malicious data through unexpected use or prompt injection attacks, which can degrade the foundation model's performance. Input filtering, which uses a rule-based engine or another AI to assess inputs for quality before approving them for use, can filter out some low-quality, inaccurate, malicious, or poorly formatted inputs that could cause degradation.

source.quote: Gen AI use cases can be vulnerable to the ingestion of low-quality or malicious data

guardrails.name: Model calibration
guardrails.description: Calibration in Gen AI is an approach to system architecture which involves re-running the model repeatedly and sampling responses to determine whether they are sufficiently similar. Calibration may include the addition of small amounts of variability to the prompt in each run.

source.quote: Calibration in Gen AI is an approach to system architecture which involves re-running the model repeatedly

guardrails.name: Modular architecture
guardrails.description: Stability can be improved by adopting a modular architecture with discrete tasks performed by individual models and components. A modular architecture can be more robust against drift, because of the resilience of other components in the use case, and can be easier to maintain, because each component can be independently monitored and repaired.

source.quote: Stability can be improved by adopting a modular architecture with discrete tasks performed by individual models

guardrails.name: Reinforcement learning
guardrails.description: For AI models based on neural networks, reinforcement learning involves generating outputs and then scoring those outputs for desirability (scoring by a human is Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback, RLHF, and scoping by a machine is Reinforcement Learning with AI Feedback, RLAIF). These scores are used to adjust model weights to favour higher-scoring behaviours. Reinforcement learning can be used to enforce desirable behaviours when encountering new data types or unfamiliar situations, or can be used to improve accuracy or soundness, such as by favouring truthful responses.

source.quote: scoring by a human is Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback, RLHF

guardrails.name: Robustness testing
guardrails.description: Testing an AI against a range of input types, including by deliberately selecting noisy input data or by testing the AI against adversarial inputs. These can include assessing the AI against potential variations in its operating context, such as different market conditions than those that applied to its training data. This can be used to determine whether an AI is sufficiently robust in the face of predictable types of data drift.

source.quote: Testing an AI against a range of input types, including by deliberately selecting noisy input data

guardrails.name: Small model selection
guardrails.description: Smaller foundation models in Gen AI use cases have been observed to demonstrate improved stability and reliability, at the potential cost of decreased performance. Selecting a smaller model where appropriate, and where that model provides sufficient performance, can increase the stability and predictability in diverse usage contexts.

source.quote: Smaller foundation models in Gen AI use cases have been observed to demonstrate improved stability and reliability

guardrails.name: Weight regularisation and normalisation
guardrails.description: Potential causes of instability or data drift in neural network-based use cases include overfitting or low rates of convergence. These can be addressed by regularising parameters, reducing the largest weights, or by normalising the inputs between layers, which can reduce model instability and encourage a more narrow, predictable band of outputs.

source.quote: Potential causes of instability or data drift in neural network-based use cases include overfitting or low rates of convergence.

guardrails.name: Synthetic evaluation datasets
guardrails.description: Generating controlled datasets with known properties can facilitate testing and validation for AI use cases. In particular, the generation of synthetic edge cases or other rare scenarios may enable testing under conditions that are underrepresented in real data.

source.quote: Generating controlled datasets with known properties can facilitate testing and validation for AI use cases.

guardrails.name: Jailbreak detection
guardrails.description: See "input filtering" under "Robustness and Stability".

source.quote: See "input filtering" under "Robustness and Stability".

guardrails.name: Penetration testing
guardrails.description: Penetration testing, often referred to as "pen testing," is a proactive security assessment where authorised professionals simulate a cyberattack. The primary goal of a pen test is to identify vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, or weaknesses before malicious actors can exploit them. Pen testing involves employing real-world attack techniques, including exploiting known vulnerabilities and identifying potential zero-day threats, to test the robustness of a system's security controls. The test is performed in a controlled environment to ensure that no harm is caused to the system or its users.

source.quote: Penetration testing, often referred to as "pen testing," is a proactive security assessment

guardrails.name: Red teaming
guardrails.description: Red Teaming is an advanced security testing process where ethical hackers simulate real-world cyberattacks to uncover vulnerabilities, assess organisational defences, and improve security operations. Unlike traditional penetration testing, it takes a holistic approach, evaluating systems, processes, and personnel. In AI, red teaming is used to identify and mitigate risks such as data leaks, biased or toxic outputs, and adversarial manipulation, ensuring models are safe, reliable, and ethical. This proactive method enhances security readiness, operational resilience, and compliance with regulatory standards while safeguarding both cybersecurity and AI system. It is particularly useful for Gen AI systems.

source.quote: Red Teaming is an advanced security testing process where ethical hackers simulate real-world cyberattacks

guardrails.name: Role-based access controls
guardrails.description: These are access management mechanisms that restrict system permissions based on a user's job role within an organisation. They ensure individuals can only access the data and functions necessary for their responsibilities, reducing the risk of unauthorised actions or data breaches.

source.quote: access management mechanisms that restrict system permissions based on a user's job role within an organisation

guardrails.name: Vulnerability assessment
guardrails.description: Vulnerability assessments are conducted to evaluate and prioritise security risks in software, applications, and networks. These are typically recurring, automated scans that search for known vulnerabilities in a system and flag them for review. Security teams use vulnerability assessments to quickly check for common flaws. The following methodologies are commonly applied: • System Analysis: Both dynamic and static analysis techniques are employed to examine the application. These methods uncover coding errors in systems, whether they are operational or dormant. • Dependency Vulnerability Scans: Attackers may exploit weaknesses in external code components, such as libraries and binaries. These scans help identify vulnerabilities tied to specific versions of these dependencies, enabling proactive mitigation.

source.quote: Vulnerability assessments are conducted to evaluate and prioritise security risks in software, applications, and networks.

interpretability_typology.name: Inherent interpretability
interpretability_typology.definition: Some types of models, especially those with low dimensionality or that create outputs as a weighted sum of inputs (such as a linear regression), are inherently interpretable. Models built using decision trees, decision sets, or rule-based classifiers are also considered inherently interpretable. The selection of such a model significantly enhances explainability.

source.quote: Some types of models, especially those with low dimensionality or that create outputs as a weighted sum of inputs

interpretability_typology.name: Interpretability constraints
interpretability_typology.definition: AI with interpretability constraints are systems whose characteristics have been modified to improve their interpretability, sometimes at the cost of a penalty to performance. Interpretability constraints include rule-based reasoning or measures to sparsify neural networks.

source.quote: Interpretability constraints include rule-based reasoning or measures to sparsify neural networks.

interpretability_typology.definition: Post-hoc interpretability techniques support the analysis of black box models by attempting to assess how an output was created. These techniques vary in complexity and applicability to different model architectures. Such techniques consist of building surrogate models, generating Shapley values, or assessing deep learning models using gradient-based assessments.

source.quote: Such techniques consist of building surrogate models, generating Shapley values, or assessing deep learning models

considerations.title: Ensure that an AI governance and risk management operating model is clearly defined by leveraging and, as needed, uplifting the roles and capabilities of existing enterprise functions including relevant roles from the Board, Senior Management, and operational governance, with sufficient operating effectiveness measures in place to support them. (1.2)

implementation_practices.text: Embed additional responsibilities for AI governance and risk management, as required, in relevant Board and Senior Management roles.

source.quote: Embed additional responsibilities for AI governance and risk management, as required

implementation_practices.text: Ensure that operational governance functions have clear roles and responsibilities assigned to operationalise AI governance and risk management activities across the enterprise.

source.quote: operational governance functions have clear roles and responsibilities assigned to operationalise

implementation_practices.text: Ensure that existing governance processes, forums, assets, and tools are updated to effectively enable AI governance and risk management.

source.quote: existing governance processes, forums, assets, and tools are updated to effectively enable

implementation_practices.text: Ensure that sufficient operating effectiveness and horizon-scanning measures are in place to monitor and improve the AI governance and risk management operating model over time.

source.quote: sufficient operating effectiveness and horizon-scanning measures are in place to monitor
Consideration 1. Ensure that an AI governance and risk management operating model is clearly defined

considerations.title: Ensure that governance documents define key AI-related concepts, processes, and responsibilities, and that they remain up-to-date and effective in supporting all aspects of the FI’s approach to AI governance and risk management (2.1).

implementation_practices.text: Ensure robust conceptual foundations for AI governance and risk management by establishing AI principles, defining key AI-related concepts, establishing frameworks for effective AI identification, and continuously improving these foundations over time as necessary.

source.quote: Ensure robust conceptual foundations for AI governance and risk management by establishing AI principles

implementation_practices.text: Ensure that all aspects of AI governance and risk management are effectively institutionalised throughout the FI’s governance documents, and that a process is in place to periodically review and reassess them.

source.quote: effectively institutionalised throughout the FI’s governance documents, and that a process is in place
Consideration 2. Ensure that governance documents define key AI-related concepts, processes, and responsibilities

considerations.title: Enhance the organisational risk framework and risk appetite to include enterprise risks, strategies, and key risk indicators (KRIs) that track, monitor, and mitigate AI-specific risks (2.2).

implementation_practices.text: Identify the new or enhanced risks of AI that are relevant to the enterprise and ensure that the enterprise risk taxonomy effectively captures them.

source.quote: Identify the new or enhanced risks of AI that are relevant to the enterprise

implementation_practices.text: Assess existing enterprise risk controls for their fitness in addressing AI-specific enterprise risks, and uplift those controls where gaps exist.

source.quote: Assess existing enterprise risk controls for their fitness in addressing AI-specific enterprise risks

implementation_practices.text: Ensure that key risk indicators (KRIs) are in place to measure AI-specific risks and that relevant incidents, issues, or risk events are appropriately tracked and managed.

source.quote: key risk indicators (KRIs) are in place to measure AI-specific risks

implementation_practices.text: Ensure that effective monitoring is in place to identify AI-specific risk events or breaches of KRI thresholds to a degree proportionate to the FI’s risk appetite.

source.quote: effective monitoring is in place to identify AI-specific risk events or breaches of KRI thresholds
Consideration 3. Enhance the organisational risk framework and risk appetite to include enterprise risks

source.section: Select New Challenges and Potential Risks of Agentic AI
source.quote: The technical complexity of agentic systems – which can orchestrate numerous AI agents

agentic_risk_factors.description: Alignment with human intentions is a well-known existing challenge for AI; the complexity of agentic architectures and their use for more complex tasks over longer time horizons makes alignment more challenging.

source.section: Select New Challenges and Potential Risks of Agentic AI
source.quote: Alignment with human intentions is a well-known existing challenge for AI.

agentic_risk_factors.description: Complex interactions between components, especially between different agents, are difficult to predict; even where individual agents behave within acceptable parameters, emergent behaviours could lead to unintended or undesirable outputs.

source.section: Select New Challenges and Potential Risks of Agentic AI
source.quote: emergent behaviours from systems of individually performant agents could lead to unintended or undesirable outputs

agentic_risk_factors.description: In complex agentic systems, especially those with multiple interconnected agents, the number of points of failure increases non-linearly, and errors in one agent or component could cause unpredictable or unwanted behaviour overall.

source.quote: the number of points of failure increases non-linearly

gen_ai_vs_agentic.gen_ai: Gen AI systems like RAG-based chatbots are not typically referred to as Agentic AI due to their relatively low levels of autonomy.
gen_ai_vs_agentic.agentic_ai: Agentic AI describes systems that include components for making plans and for taking action, often involving tools that interact with their environment.

source.quote: Gen AI systems like RAG-based chatbots are not typically referred to as Agentic AI due to their relatively low levels of autonomy.

gen_ai_vs_agentic.gen_ai: Non-Agentic AI: Gen AI with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) – an LLM chatbot with basic retrieval capabilities from a static knowledge base (user prompt/response, search/summary of knowledge base).
gen_ai_vs_agentic.agentic_ai: Agentic AI: a single agent with reasoning capability (LLM-based agent with reasoning and structured actions, using internal workflows for planning, action, memory and tools), and multiple agents collaborating and delegating (a generalist agent orchestrating specialist, supervisor and learning agents for end-to-end automation); characterised by more autonomy, more planning, more independent action and more complex capabilities.

source.quote: Figure 5.0.1: Stylised Comparison of Gen AI and Agentic AI Architectures

gen_ai_vs_agentic.gen_ai: Gen AI was primarily constrained to content creation, summary, or retrieval tasks.
gen_ai_vs_agentic.agentic_ai: Agentic AI can take complex, multi-step actions, creating plans from high-level natural language directions and executing them using connected tools; it can undertake tasks that could never before be automated, representing a substantial maturation of Gen AI.

source.quote: a substantial maturation of Gen AI, which was primarily constrained to content creation, summary, or retrieval tasks

gen_ai_vs_agentic.gen_ai: Gen AI systems were primarily reactive in nature, relying on users to take actions on their advice.
gen_ai_vs_agentic.agentic_ai: Agentic systems have the potential to be proactive, to effect real-world states directly, and to offload tasks not well-suited to AI to other software tools (e.g. passing mathematical tasks to a traditional calculator).

source.quote: Where Gen AI systems were primarily reactive in nature, agentic systems have the potential to be proactive

gen_ai_vs_agentic.gen_ai: Losing context on broader and more complex tasks is a major limiting factor for LLM utility.
gen_ai_vs_agentic.agentic_ai: Agentic systems can, through their memory and planning functions, take on broader and more complex tasks without losing context.

source.quote: take on broader and more complex tasks without losing context, which is otherwise a major limiting factor for LLM utility

gen_ai_vs_agentic.gen_ai: A known challenge in business adoption of Gen AI is its tendency to commit errors or outright hallucinate information, which can make it risky for critical use cases.
gen_ai_vs_agentic.agentic_ai: While errors and hallucinations also occur, multi-step reasoning processes or built-in error checking give agentic systems greater potential to catch their own errors, and their multiple steps and components lend themselves to guardrail modules (PII screening, toxicity detection, fact-checking).

source.quote: the introduction of multi-step reasoning processes or built-in error checking gives agentic systems a greater potential to identify and catch their own errors

gen_ai_vs_agentic.aspect: Materiality/complexity of workflows suited to the technology
gen_ai_vs_agentic.gen_ai: Prior AI architectures could tackle less complex, lower-materiality workflows.
gen_ai_vs_agentic.agentic_ai: Agentic systems are currently well-suited to tackling more complex, higher-materiality workflows than prior AI architectures could.

illustrations.title: Income Insurance: Integrating AI Governance with Risk Policy
